context: Let’s pretend the glass has got all soft like gauze
mainIdea: Alice imagines Looking-glass House and pretends the glass is soft. Then the glass really begins to melt like mist.
simple: Alice asks the kitten if it would like to live in Looking-glass House. She wonders if they would give it milk there, and she thinks that Looking-glass milk may not be good to drink. Then she talks about the passage. If you leave the door of their drawing room wide open, you can see a little of the passage in Looking-glass House. It is very like their passage as far as you can see, but it may be quite different further on. She says how nice it would be to get through into the house, and she is sure it has beautiful things in it. She says, let us pretend there is a way to get through, and that the glass has gone soft like gauze. Then she says the glass is turning into a sort of mist. She is up on the chimneypiece as she speaks, though she hardly knows how she got there. And the glass really is beginning to melt away, like a bright silver mist.

context: ’Twas brillig, and the slithy toves Did gyre and gimble in the wabe
mainIdea: This is the poem Jabberwocky. It has many made-up words. It tells how a boy kills a creature called the Jabberwock.
simple: The poem has many made-up words, so some of its parts are not clear. It begins with a scene that has strange creatures in it, and the creatures have made-up names. Then someone speaks to a boy, calling him "my son". He tells him to beware of the Jabberwock, which has jaws that bite and claws that catch. He also tells him to beware of the Jubjub bird and to keep away from the Bandersnatch. The boy takes his sword in his hand and looks for the enemy for a long time. He rests by the Tumtum tree and stands there for a while, thinking. While he stands there, the Jabberwock comes through the wood with eyes of flame, making noises as it comes. The boy hits it again and again with his sword and leaves it dead. He goes back with its head. Then the speaker asks if the boy has killed the Jabberwock and tells him to come to his arms. The speaker shouts glad words about the day and laughs in his joy. The poem ends with the same words that it began with.

context: if I don’t make haste I shall have to go back
mainIdea: Alice runs out of the room and floats down the stairs without touching them. She is glad to walk again in the usual way.
simple: Alice thinks that she must hurry, or she will have to go back through the Looking-glass before she has seen the rest of the house. She says she will look at the garden first. In a moment she is out of the room and goes down the stairs. At least it is not exactly running. It is a new way that she has invented for getting down the stairs quickly and easily. She keeps only the tips of her fingers on the handrail and floats gently down, and her feet do not touch the stairs. Then she floats through the hall. She would have gone straight out of the door in the same way, but she catches hold of the doorpost. She is getting a little giddy from so much floating in the air. She is rather glad to find herself walking again in the natural way.

context: never changed their places at all: however fast they went
mainIdea: Alice and the Queen run fast, but the trees do not move past them. The Queen tells Alice not to talk.
simple: The strangest part was that the trees and the other things around them never changed their places. However fast they went, they never seemed to pass anything. Poor, puzzled Alice thought, "I wonder if all the things move along with us?" The Queen seemed to guess what she was thinking, and she cried, "Faster! Do not try to talk!"

context: it takes all the running you can do, to keep in the same place
mainIdea: The Red Queen says that in her country you must run as fast as you can just to stay in one place. To go somewhere else, you must run twice as fast.
simple: The Queen says it is a slow sort of country. She tells Alice that here you must do all the running you can just to stay in the same place. If you want to get somewhere else, you must run at least twice as fast as that.

context: I’ve heard nonsense, compared with which that would be as sensible as a dictionary
mainIdea: The Red Queen shakes her head. She says she has heard nonsense that was so much worse that this would seem as sensible as a dictionary.
simple: The Red Queen shook her head. She told Alice that she may call it nonsense if she likes. But the Queen said she had heard nonsense, and if you compare that nonsense with this, this would seem as sensible as a dictionary.
